a170.speaker: Alem Teklegergis, Chairman of the Holidays Coordinating Committee
a170.name: Alem Teklegergis
a170.title: Chairman of the Holidays Coordinating Committee
a170.speech: Said that Eritrean festivals, beyond being public gatherings, make a significant contribution in strengthening unity and attachment to the homeland, as well as in nurturing nationalism and noble societal values; indicating that the Eritrean festival in the Scandinavian countries plays a vital role in preserving national values, he added that the successful implementation of the festivals attests to the strong and committed participation of nationals and the effective organization of the community.

a224.speaker: Police Situation report, Otan Ayegbaju Division (Nigeria Police)
a224.name: Police Situation report
a224.title: Otan Ayegbaju Division (Nigeria Police)
a224.speech: Confirmed the incident; identified two other persons who are currently receiving treatment in an undisclosed hospital as Mr Solomon Kingsley and Chief Olusegun Alalade all of Alalade compound Ada; noted the victim had been deposited at the Healthy Paradise Mutuary Ikirun for autopsy. It reads partly: "Today Friday 18/04/2025 X SUD X at about 1645 HRS X there was a complaint from one Babasanjo Alalade M X of Alalade compound Ada X Osun State... On getting to the farm they were attacked by bunch of bees X and as a result x Mr Abideen Olabiyi ( M) X lost his life x while the other two victims manage to escape with their lives X detectives mine visited the scene X photograph taken X corps removed and deposited at Healthy Paradise Mutuary Ikirun for autopsy while the other two victims were rushed to undisclose hospital at Ada for treatment x for your information sir X From Supol Otan Ayegbaju Division."

a224.speaker: Babasanjo Alalade, complainant and relative of the victims (cited in the police report)
a224.name: Babasanjo Alalade
a224.title: complainant and relative of the victims (cited in the police report)
a224.speech: "he stated that today X three of his brothers went to farm X one Abideen Olabiyi M X Mr Solomon Kingsley X and Chief Olusegun Alalade x all of Alalade compound Ada X went to the farm in Olobe Farm Igbajo."

a224.speaker: SaharaReporters
a224.name: SaharaReporters
a224.speech: SaharaReporters gathered that the incident happened on Friday, April 18, 2025 at the Olobe Farm, Igbajo.

a235.speaker: US Embassy in Mogadishu (statement)
a235.name: US Embassy in Mogadishu (statement)
a235.speech: "This $1.1 billion in debt relief is in addition to the $1.2 billion of development, economic, security, and humanitarian assistance the United States has provided to Somalia just this fiscal year. The United States continues to be a steadfast partner in support of the people of Somalia."

a235.speaker: Government of Somalia (announcement)
a235.name: Government of Somalia (announcement)
a235.speech: Announced that the loans, around a quarter of what it owes, have been cancelled as part of a series of agreements.

a311.speaker: South African Department of Health contingency plan circular (document, sent to provincial health departments on 11 February)
a311.name: South African Department of Health contingency plan circular (document
a311.title: sent to provincial health departments on 11 February)
a311.speech: Says patients who qualify for a supply of six months of treatment at a time must have a suppressed viral load for “two consecutive periods” ; says only people who already get their drugs for three months at a time can be considered for a six-month supply, and only if the clinic has enough stock of the entry-level three-in-one pill, TLD.

a311.speaker: South African Department of Health contingency plan circular (document, sent to provincial health departments on 11 February)
a311.name: South African Department of Health contingency plan circular (document
a311.title: sent to provincial health departments on 11 February)
a311.speech: Says all clients older than six months should, during this crisis period, get an ARV supply of at least three months if they don't experience complications, and that HIV-negative people who want the daily anti-HIV pill should get a three-month supply along with HIV self-tests ; includes as another “coping strategy” allowing people who collect treatment at community pick-up points such as churches, mosques, private pharmacies or adherence clubs a 28-day grace period to fetch it, still qualifying for automatic script renewal.

a311.speaker: Ramphelane Morewane, acting deputy director-general for HIV, South African Department of Health
a311.name: Ramphelane Morewane
a311.title: acting deputy director-general for HIV, South African Department of Health
a311.speech: Told Bhekisisa that the longest period for which government patients currently receive ARVs at a time is three months, and shared Department of Health figures showing that of South Africa's 5.8-million people on ARVs, 5.417-million are state patients, of whom 1.6-million (around 30%) get their medicine for three months at a time.

a311.speaker: Ramphelane Morewane, acting deputy director-general for HIV, South African Department of Health
a311.name: Ramphelane Morewane
a311.title: acting deputy director-general for HIV, South African Department of Health
a311.speech: Says about half - 2.7-million of the state's 5.4-million ARV patients - received their medication outside a health facility by the end of 2024, and that “the sudden withdrawal of Pepfar could slow us down on this goal” ; “But it won't cause a total disruption, because we don't exclusively depend on Pepfar.”

a311.speaker: Ramphelane Morewane, acting deputy director-general for HIV, South African Department of Health
a311.name: Ramphelane Morewane
a311.title: acting deputy director-general for HIV, South African Department of Health
a311.speech: Says the health department hasn't so far received reports of people on ARVs being unable to get their treatment from, at the very least, a different public health facility.

a311.speaker: South African health department spokesperson
a311.name: South African health department spokesperson
a311.speech: Says giving HIV-negative people a three-month supply of the anti-HIV pill has mostly already been happening, and that the department's goal is to get around 700 000 new HIV-negative people to use the anti-HIV pill at least once.

a311.speaker: South African health department spokesperson
a311.name: South African health department spokesperson
a311.speech: Confirmed that six PrEP research sites - two in Johannesburg and four in Lejweleputswa in the Free State - which were part of the Catalyst study and funded by Pepfar via USAID, have closed down.

a311.speaker: Francois Venter, HIV researcher who heads the organisation Ezintsha at Wits University
a311.name: Francois Venter
a311.title: HIV researcher who heads the organisation Ezintsha at Wits University
a311.speech: “Stopping such studies so abruptly is unethical, a huge waste of time and resources, and a violation of trust. It's extremely complicated - and expensive - to restart them.”

a311.speaker: Devex (news report)
a311.name: Devex (news report)
a311.speech: Reports that even in cases in other countries where waivers had been approved, the Trump administration hasn't made the funds for those activities available, because the online payment system was disabled or the remaining USAID staff had been locked out of their emails.

a311.speaker: US court ruling (late Thursday)
a311.name: US court ruling (late Thursday)
a311.speech: Instructed President Trump's administration to temporarily unfreeze all foreign assistance funding, including Pepfar funds that reach projects through USAID, effectively cancelling the waivers and allowing projects to revert to their original grants.

a311.speaker: US federal judge (temporary restraining order)
a311.name: US federal judge (temporary restraining order)
a311.speech: Enforced a temporary restraining order blocking Trump's administration from freezing federal grants, after which Pepfar projects funded through the CDC restarted.

a311.speaker: Mitchell Warren, head of the New York-based advocacy organisation Avac, one of the organisations that brought the case against the Trump administration
a311.name: Mitchell Warren
a311.title: head of the New York-based advocacy organisation Avac, one of the organisations that brought the case against the Trump administration
a311.speech: “The finding itself does not restart foreign assistance.” ; “We know that this administration seems to be beholden only to their own thinking and not to the rule of law.”

a311.speaker: Manager at one Pepfar-funded organisation (anonymous, spoke to Bhekisisa on condition of anonymity)
a311.name: Manager at one Pepfar-funded organisation (anonymous
a311.title: spoke to Bhekisisa on condition of anonymity)
a311.speech: “A major challenge has been the absence of clear leadership - not just from the national health department, but also from Pepfar.” ; “Instead of a structured, coordinated approach, implementation partners have been left to navigate an uncertain landscape with little direction, forced to answer difficult questions from provincial health officials; questions that, in many cases, simply have no clear answers.”

a311.speaker: Right to Care (guidance document distributed to workers and provincial health departments)
a311.name: Right to Care (guidance document distributed to workers and provincial health departments)
a311.speech: Warns workers throughout to keep a low profile - and to effectively self-censor.

a311.speaker: One person working in the sector (anonymous)
a311.name: One person working in the sector (anonymous)
a311.speech: “The fear was that speaking out would trigger retaliation and jeopardise any further funding. My gut said the opposite - speak out, but I remained silent, not for myself, but to protect our staff and partners.” ; “Yet, that silence felt and still feels like complicity and I'm battling shame about adhering to collective silence. Can we truly call ourselves humanitarians if we choose the safe, comfortable corner of silence over solidarity with the communities we serve?”

a369.speaker: Prof. Francisca Mutapi, Professor in Global Health Infection and Immunity and co-Director of the Global Health Academy, University of Edinburgh
a369.name: Prof. Francisca Mutapi
a369.title: Professor in Global Health Infection and Immunity and co-Director of the Global Health Academy, University of Edinburgh
a369.speech: Suggests four ways to end Africa's dependence on foreign aid for health: diversifying domestic resource mobilisation including commodity taxation such as tobacco taxes (citing Zimbabwe's 3% Aids levy started in 1999 and Nigeria's absorption of 28,000 health workers formerly paid by USAid); more private-public partnerships (citing the 2015 partnership between the Kenyan government and GE Healthcare); promotion of regional integration to boost local production (citing the African Union's harmonised Africa Medicines Authority registration facility); and leveraging development finance institutions such as the Africa Development Bank, African Export-Import Bank and the Development Bank of Southern Africa (citing the AfricInvest investment platform, which has raised over US$100 million for health investment in Africa and funded at least 45 dialysis facilities delivering over 130,000 dialysis sessions annually). She says a combination of these approaches at national, regional and continental level will accelerate Africa's withdrawal from aid dependency.

a369.speaker: Prof. Francisca Mutapi, Professor in Global Health Infection and Immunity and co-Director of the Global Health Academy, University of Edinburgh
a369.name: Prof. Francisca Mutapi
a369.title: Professor in Global Health Infection and Immunity and co-Director of the Global Health Academy, University of Edinburgh
a369.speech: Writes: "I'm a global health expert who sits on various funding and advisory boards, including those of the World Health Organisation (WHO), the UK government and boards of global resource mobilisation organisations. I am well aware of the competing funding priorities for international funders and have long advocated for local, sustainable health funding mechanisms." She argues long-term strategies to reduce aid dependency are critical, that President Donald Trump's actions have highlighted Africa's reliance on foreign aid for health funding, that foreign aid has helped but clearly leaves African countries vulnerable to the political mood swings among funders and leads to loss of self-determination over health priorities, producing single-disease focused, poorly integrated health services; and that the continent cannot continue on the same path while hoping for different outcomes.

a593.speaker: Representatives of the organising institutions (MENFOP, MTRA/ANEFIP, Djibouti Chamber of Commerce, USAID-funded PED project)
a593.name: Representatives of the organising institutions (MENFOP
a593.title: MTRA/ANEFIP, Djibouti Chamber of Commerce, USAID-funded PED project)
a593.speech: Stressed the importance of internships for young Djiboutians seeking to acquire the skills required by employers, as well as the benefits for employers of having a pool of young talent.

a593.speaker: All the partners (speakers: Mohamed Abdallah Mahyoub, Secretary General of MENFOP; Abdallah Ali Mohamed, Secretary General of MTRA; and Laura Dillon-Binkley, PED project head)
a593.name: All the partners (speakers: Mohamed Abdallah Mahyoub
a593.title: Secretary General of MENFOP; Abdallah Ali Mohamed, Secretary General of MTRA; and Laura Dillon-Binkley, PED project head)
a593.speech: Reiterated in their remarks the added value of bringing together education and labour-market actors in order to support workforce development initiatives adapted to the labour market.

a593.speaker: Interns and employers
a593.name: Interns and employers
a593.speech: Attested to the benefits they derived from the internships.

a593.speaker: MENFOP and ANEFIP (Ministry of National Education and Vocational Training; National Agency for Employment, Training and Professional Integration)
a593.name: MENFOP and ANEFIP (Ministry of National Education and Vocational Training; National Agency for Employment
a593.title: Training and Professional Integration)
a593.speech: Described their structures as well as the challenges and opportunities they see in supporting the placement of young people in internships.

a765.speaker: Dr. Viros Al-Haj, medical doctor at Yambio State Hospital
a765.name: Dr. Viros Al-Haj
a765.title: medical doctor at Yambio State Hospital
a765.speech: “Most of the cases here are malaria, and many of them are children,” she explains. “Every day, we receive at least 15 new cases of malaria, and many are diagnosed with pneumonia as well.”

a765.speaker: Dr. Viros Al-Haj, medical doctor at Yambio State Hospital
a765.name: Dr. Viros Al-Haj
a765.title: medical doctor at Yambio State Hospital
a765.speech: Notes, “Sometimes we have malaria drugs, but often we don’t. Recently, we received a consignment, but in many cases, patients have to buy the drugs from outside because they’re not available here.”

a765.speaker: Dr. Viros Al-Haj, medical doctor at Yambio State Hospital
a765.name: Dr. Viros Al-Haj
a765.title: medical doctor at Yambio State Hospital
a765.speech: “We need more anti-malaria drugs, oxygen supplies for pneumonia cases, and more diagnostic tools,” she says. “The situation is dire, but with the right resources, we can save more lives.”

a765.speaker: Dr. Najib James, doctor in the outpatient department at Yambio State Hospital
a765.name: Dr. Najib James
a765.title: doctor in the outpatient department at Yambio State Hospital
a765.speech: Highlights the prevalence of malaria among children under five, calling it one of the most common conditions at the hospital: “Malaria affects both children and adults, but it’s especially rampant among the under-fives,” he says. “Pneumonia is another major concern, and it affects many of our young patients.”

a765.speaker: Dr. Najib James, doctor in the outpatient department at Yambio State Hospital
a765.name: Dr. Najib James
a765.title: doctor in the outpatient department at Yambio State Hospital
a765.speech: Reports an increase in pneumonia cases, with many children arriving at the hospital with difficulty breathing, high fevers, and severe chest infections: “Pneumonia under five is very common, and we’re seeing over 150 different cases a day. But malaria remains the most common.”

a765.speaker: Justin, lab technician at Yambio State Hospital
a765.name: Justin
a765.title: lab technician at Yambio State Hospital
a765.speech: “We’re running out of reagents, and the lack of supplies makes it harder to conduct tests. We also don’t have enough lab technicians—there are only 10 of us, and we’re spread across many departments.”

a765.speaker: Grace Peter, mother of two children being treated for severe malaria
a765.name: Grace Peter
a765.title: mother of two children being treated for severe malaria
a765.speech: “When I came here, I was told the hospital had no malaria medicine,” she recalls. “I had to go out and find money to buy the drugs from a pharmacy. It’s not easy, but my children’s lives depend on it.”

a765.speaker: Anna Joseph, mother of a two-year-old son fighting pneumonia
a765.name: Anna Joseph
a765.title: mother of a two-year-old son fighting pneumonia
a765.speech: “The doctors are doing their best, but there isn’t enough medicine or equipment,” she says. “We just pray our children survive.”

a765.speaker: Dr. Konjo Samuel, Director of Yambio State Hospital
a765.name: Dr. Konjo Samuel
a765.title: Director of Yambio State Hospital
a765.speech: Explains that the lack of resources is a key challenge in addressing the rising number of cases: “The main issues are financing, and we’re falling behind on renovations and improvements. We’re also facing shortages of medical supplies, particularly for the laboratory and malaria treatments. Most of the consignment we receive is for antibiotics, and the anti-malaria drugs are insufficient.”

a765.speaker: Peter Ambaiyo, UNICEF Officer in Charge of Greater Equatoria
a765.name: Peter Ambaiyo
a765.title: UNICEF Officer in Charge of Greater Equatoria
a765.speech: Credits the Health Sector Transformation Project for the recent improvements at Yambio Hospital: “Since the Health Sector Transformation Project began, we’ve seen improvements in staffing, drug supplies, and overall healthcare delivery,” he explains. “It’s ensuring that communities have access to primary health care, and complicated cases are referred to secondary care.”

a879.speaker: Medical sources in the Gaza Strip
a879.name: Medical sources in the Gaza Strip
a879.speech: Said that 11 cancer patients in the Strip have been forcibly cut off from treatment and appropriate health care, as the Israeli occupation continues to prevent the entry of medical supplies and medicines ; stated that intravenous chemotherapy and medical follow-up services for cancer patients have been completely suspended in the Gaza Strip, noting that the evacuation of the European Hospital and the Cancer Centre in Gaza has worsened the catastrophic situation of the patients ; noted that 5 cancer patients require urgent referral abroad for treatment, whether for diagnosis or for chemotherapy and radiotherapy, especially given the lack of equipment for early diagnosis, and that 64% of cancer medicines are lacking, stressing that cancer patients in the Gaza Strip are now trapped in catastrophic health, social, psychological and economic conditions.

a1119.speaker: New Patriotic Party (NPP)
a1119.name: New Patriotic Party (NPP)
a1119.speech: As the incumbent party, NPP has partnered with a private entity to launch a streaming app, positioning it as a game-changer for Ghanaian music, with grand promises to prioritise local content, amplify the reach of Ghanaian artistes, and improve revenue retention within the music industry.

a1119.speaker: Abeiku Santana, National Democratic Congress (NDC) party communicator
a1119.name: Abeiku Santana
a1119.title: National Democratic Congress (NDC) party communicator
a1119.speech: Is at the forefront, arguing that a pay-per-view television platform would allow viewers to pay directly for content, with a focus on live events and shows that showcase Ghanaian entertainers.

a1119.speaker: National Democratic Congress (NDC)
a1119.name: National Democratic Congress (NDC)
a1119.speech: Claims this model would provide more direct compensation for artistes while offering new avenues for monetising live performances.

a1119.speaker: Abeiku Santana, National Democratic Congress (NDC) party communicator
a1119.name: Abeiku Santana
a1119.title: National Democratic Congress (NDC) party communicator
a1119.speech: Santana's dismissal of NPP's streaming platform as a 'lie' that won't benefit the industry is a classic example of the knee-jerk partisanship that often plagues Ghanaian politics.

a1229.speaker: Mao Zedong, former Chairman of the Communist Party of China
a1229.name: Mao Zedong
a1229.title: former Chairman of the Communist Party of China
a1229.speech: likened the United States Imperialism to a “paper tiger” ; “In appearance it is very powerful but in reality it is nothing to be afraid of, it is a paper tiger. Outwardly a tiger, it is made of paper, unable to withstand the wind and the rain. I believe the United States is nothing but a paper tiger.”

a1229.speaker: Julius Kambarage Nyerere, Chairman of the South Commission
a1229.name: Julius Kambarage Nyerere
a1229.title: Chairman of the South Commission
a1229.speech: said “we cannot, unlike other countries, send rockets to the moon. But we can send rockets of love and hope to all our fellow humans wherever they may be.”

a1229.speaker: Dr Dambisa Moyo, Zambian economist (book “Dead Aid”)
a1229.name: Dr Dambisa Moyo
a1229.title: Zambian economist (book “Dead Aid”)
a1229.speech: cited as the source of the concept of the west’s “dead aid”, the recurrent trap that Lesotho should avoid.

a1229.speaker: Hans Morgenthau, United States political scientist, father of the realist theory of international relations
a1229.name: Hans Morgenthau
a1229.title: United States political scientist, father of the realist theory of international relations
a1229.speech: pointed out that “foreign aid is no different from diplomatic or military policy or propaganda. They are all weapons in the political armory of the nation.”

a1229.speaker: Thomas Dichter, former Peace Corps member and country director (article in Foreign Service Journal)
a1229.name: Thomas Dichter
a1229.title: former Peace Corps member and country director (article in Foreign Service Journal)
a1229.speech: pointed out that it is commonly criticized that if the key variables for development, including cultural, social and political realms, are not present, aid will not only be ineffective but also create dependency.

a1229.speaker: China
a1229.name: China
a1229.speech: in July 2023 put forward a four-point proposal on strengthening cooperation among the countries of the Global South, that is, they should work together on eliminating conflict and building peace, restoring vitality and promoting development, being open and inclusive and seeking common progress, and achieving unity and cooperation.

a1229.speaker: Xi Jinping, General Secretary of the Communist Party of China
a1229.name: Xi Jinping
a1229.title: General Secretary of the Communist Party of China
a1229.speech: has proposed the Global Development Initiative (GDI), Global Security Initiative (GSI) and Global Civilization Initiative (GCI), giving further response to the universal aspiration of all peoples for peace, development and cooperation, and offering China’s solutions to the common problems facing humanity today.

a1229.speaker: Kwame Nkrumah, late President of Ghana
a1229.name: Kwame Nkrumah
a1229.title: late President of Ghana
a1229.speech: posited that “For my part, I must say that as long as I live, and as long as any little vestige of colonialism and imperialism remains in Africa, I shall prosecute a ruthless war on these monsters, a war in which there shall be no truce. Colonialism and imperialism have no honour, no shame, no morals and conscience.”

a1289.speaker: Tokpah John Mulbah, Chairperson of the Rubber Development Fund Incorporated (RDFI)
a1289.name: Tokpah John Mulbah
a1289.title: Chairperson of the Rubber Development Fund Incorporated (RDFI)
a1289.speech: outlined key challenges facing the industry, including limited funding for smallholder farmers, outdated infrastructure, and fluctuating global markets. Emphasis was placed on empowering smallholder farmers through enhanced training, modern equipment access, and financial resources. He highlighted Gbarnga's strategic location in Liberia's agricultural landscape and how this venue was ideal for the conference. ; "We want to use this gathering to explore opportunities for diversifying the industry by increasing local processing capabilities, which could create jobs and add economic value to Liberia's rubber exports," Mulbah noted. "We, as industry leaders, are optimistic that new initiatives such as the RDFI and other viable initiatives will provide the support needed to modernize the sector and make it more competitive internationally."

a1289.speaker: Dr. Alexander Nuetah, Liberian Agriculture Minister
a1289.name: Dr. Alexander Nuetah
a1289.title: Liberian Agriculture Minister
a1289.speech: acknowledged the sector's underperformance and outlined the government's commitment to identifying and resolving the root causes; noted that the intent of the government is to discover the problems that is causing the under performance of the rubber sector. "We want to see a future where the rubber industry will be a vibrant one because it remains the largest export earner in the agriculture sector and if we cannot make it work we will not create jobs, we will not create the foreign exchanges that we need to run this country," he said. ; "Rubber is one of Liberia's most valuable exports, generating substantial foreign exchange that supports national reserves and stabilizes the economy. By selling rubber products abroad, Liberia earns foreign currency that helps balance trade deficits and funds public projects."

a1289.speaker: Dr. Alexander Nuetah, Liberian Agriculture Minister
a1289.name: Dr. Alexander Nuetah
a1289.title: Liberian Agriculture Minister
a1289.speech: referenced the establishment of a national rubber sector steering committee to address industry challenges and support smallholder farmers and concessionaires; said the government of Liberia will be instituting the national rubber sector steering committee, which will work along with the RDFI to ensure that issues in the rubber sector are addressed. He said the steering committee will make the right decision that will help guide the government in implementing policy that will improve the sector, and revealed further that the committee will be constituted in December of this year and aims to set a purchasing price in the rubber sector of Liberia.

a1289.speaker: Stakeholders at the conference
a1289.name: Stakeholders at the conference
a1289.speech: noted that the potential of diversifying rubber processing in Liberia presents an attractive opportunity to enhance economic value retention within the country and create new job opportunities. By selling rubber products abroad, they said, Liberia not only earns vital foreign exchange but also supports local economies and alleviates poverty. ; The stakeholders also hope that the RDFI leadership after the conference will lay the groundwork for reforms and initiatives aimed at revitalizing Liberia's rubber industry, positioning it as a strategic player in both regional and international markets.

a1339.speaker: "Roll Call on Teacher Absenteeism in Namibia", a USAID/Basic Support Project study by Liman Muhammed and Tuaitiko Shikongo (study of 617 schools in six regions)
a1339.name: "Roll Call on Teacher Absenteeism in Namibia"
a1339.title: a USAID/Basic Support Project study by Liman Muhammed and Tuaitiko Shikongo (study of 617 schools in six regions)
a1339.speech: Found that the implications of teachers getting sick and staying away from school lead to the absence of instruction for long stretches, which leads to many learners not successfully completing their schooling.

a1339.speaker: "Roll Call on Teacher Absenteeism in Namibia" (report)
a1339.name: "Roll Call on Teacher Absenteeism in Namibia" (report)
a1339.speech: Notes: "By combining teachers absent due to illness, compassionate and special leave, the data shows that 74 percent of teachers were absent for reasons possibly related to the impact of HIV/AIDS on themselves and their families."

a1339.speaker: USAID/Basic Support Project (the project)
a1339.name: USAID/Basic Support Project (the project)
a1339.speech: Says the country has empirical evidence to support the notion that the HIV/AIDS epidemic is having an effect on classroom instruction in terms of time lost, and says of the findings: "We can start to develop some strategies in the schools and clusters with the greatest number of days lost to teacher illness that could serve as role models for other circuits and clusters of schools."

a1339.speaker: USAID/Basic Support Project (the project)
a1339.name: USAID/Basic Support Project (the project)
a1339.speech: Feels there is a need to work with the regions to develop a more systematic and clearer method for tracking teacher absenteeism, and made a number of proposals including training on multi-grade teaching, team planning and team work, applying for volunteers, involving parents in teaching, having enough textbooks and keeping a teacher absenteeism record.

a1339.speaker: "Roll Call on Teacher Absenteeism in Namibia" (report)
a1339.name: "Roll Call on Teacher Absenteeism in Namibia" (report)
a1339.speech: Says the number of teachers absent due to sickness results in an unacceptable number of school days lost, because if each teacher handles on average 30 periods per week, there will be a total of 344,340 periods lost in classrooms in the six target regions.

a1339.speaker: "Roll Call on Teacher Absenteeism in Namibia" (report)
a1339.name: "Roll Call on Teacher Absenteeism in Namibia" (report)
a1339.speech: Notes that there are many international and local people who would like to work as volunteers: "Depending on the needs, all schools could have volunteer teachers who are fully trained to handle teaching of most subjects in the primary curriculum."

a1427.speaker: Pamoja Salama project managers
a1427.name: Pamoja Salama project managers
a1427.speech: Commenting on the initiative, said: "The way and speed with which the virus spreads shows that no one can beat Covid-19 alone. We all need to combat the disease together. The virus can affect anyone because to the virus we are all the same."

a1427.speaker: Pamoja Salama project managers
a1427.name: Pamoja Salama project managers
a1427.speech: Emphasised that there are people who are more at risk of developing the most serious forms of the disease, namely the elderly or people who suffer from other health problems, such as diabetes, malnutrition, etc. ; "We are all responsible for protecting the most vulnerable around us. We need to take care of each other and can do so by wearing masks, washing our hands and keeping a safe distance whenever possible."

a1451.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)
a1451.name: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
a1451.title: Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)
a1451.speech: "The WHO team and partners managed to reach Al Shifa hospital today [Thursday] and deliver 9,300 litres of fuel and medical supplies to care for a thousand trauma patients and one hundred kidney dialysis patients." ; Explained that Al Shifa has partially resumed services, which "means that fuel consumption is much higher and the need for medical supplies is increasing."

a1451.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)
a1451.name: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
a1451.title: Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)
a1451.speech: In a post on the social network X, called for "sustained and safe access" in order to continue supplying medical materials, fuel, food and water to Al Shifa, which was Gaza's main hospital ; had appealed to Israel to authorise the entry of WHO staff and stressed that the main obstacle to the delivery of aid has not been the capacity of UN agencies, but rather the lack of access.

a1451.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)
a1451.name: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
a1451.title: Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)
a1451.speech: "We insist once again that health must be protected and never be a target or militarised."

a1451.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO) daily report
a1451.name: World Health Organization (WHO) daily report
a1451.speech: Revealed that it had had to cancel six missions to northern Gaza over the past two weeks, having failed to receive authorisation and security guarantees from Israel; the report detailed that missions to send emergency medical supplies to Gaza City's central pharmacy were denied on five occasions, and that the delivery of fuel needed to operate medical supply facilities was cancelled six times.

a1451.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a1451.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
a1451.speech: Lamented new attacks on health facilities in Gaza, such as the one suffered on Wednesday by a Palestinian Red Crescent ambulance, in which four of the organisation's workers and two already-injured patients died.

a1451.speaker: United Nations (UN)
a1451.name: United Nations (UN)
a1451.speech: Said on Thursday that only three of the 21 humanitarian aid missions to northern Gaza have been carried out since the beginning of January, because of delays at Israeli checkpoints and because many roads are impassable.

a1451.speaker: Ministry of Health of Gaza
a1451.name: Ministry of Health of Gaza
a1451.speech: According to the ministry, Israeli attacks have caused 23,357 deaths and 59,410 injuries since the start of the conflict in the strip on 7 October.

a1563.speaker: Hans Neumann, dean of the diplomatic corps in Benin (German ambassador)
a1563.name: Hans Neumann
a1563.title: dean of the diplomatic corps in Benin (German ambassador)
a1563.speech: Praised: "I would like to commend Beninese democracy, which showed maturity during the organisation of the marches of 10 December last, in which the entire political class behaved well." He indicated that 2015 would be decisive for the country, which would have to meet the challenge of organising legislative and communal elections: "A living and stable democracy is a guarantee of development and peace." ; "We encourage you to continue the dialogue with the political class, and the political class to play its part in preserving peace," reiterating the commitment of the country's technical and financial partners to continue their friendship and cooperation with the country. He also mentioned the government's concern to lead Benin towards progress, modernity and shared prosperity, on the basis of tolerance and permanent dialogue with all the nation's vital forces.

a1563.speaker: Boni Yayi, President of the Republic of Benin
a1563.name: Boni Yayi
a1563.title: President of the Republic of Benin
a1563.speech: Declared: "I would like here to reassure once again the entire Beninese people and the international community that my government will take all the necessary measures for the proper conduct of the coming elections." He indicated that, in terms of financing, his government had honoured all its commitments to the various bodies responsible for organising the elections.

a1563.speaker: Boni Yayi, President of the Republic of Benin
a1563.name: Boni Yayi
a1563.title: President of the Republic of Benin
a1563.speech: On regional questions, said that Benin has always reaffirmed its attachment to the bonds of brotherhood and cooperation it maintains with its immediate neighbours and the sub-region, and that the holding on 12 January of the joint Council of Ministers between the governments of Benin and Niger reflects this logic. While acknowledging that the past year was difficult for the states of the region because of economic, political and social constraints, he specified that his government worked to pursue its development programme at a more sustained pace, with the option of promoting public-private partnership; the Round Table of partners held in Paris in June 2014 enabled the country to mobilise 12 billion dollars, about 6,000 billion CFA francs, to finance certain structuring projects. He also welcomed Benin's improved ranking in the World Bank's Doing Business report, Benin's eligibility for a second Millennium Challenge Account (MCA) Compact, and Canada's reinstatement of Benin on the list of focus countries for Canadian official development assistance. "On the economic front, all the indicators are green, with a growth rate of 5.7% in 2014. Benin is among the three countries in the zone to meet all the convergence criteria within WAEMU."

a1563.speaker: Boni Yayi, President of the Republic of Benin
a1563.name: Boni Yayi
a1563.title: President of the Republic of Benin
a1563.speech: Returned to the question of the Ebola epidemic raging in Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia, welcoming the appreciable assistance of partners which today allows the situation to be brought under control in the affected areas; deplored that the African continent is still confronted with conflict situations, notably in Libya, the Central African Republic, eastern DRC, Sudan and Somalia. "Benin joins the member states of the African Union in calling for the rapid operationalisation of the African Capacity for Immediate Response to Crises, pending the complete establishment of the African Standby Force and its Rapid Deployment Capability." On a regional strategy of response against the Islamist sect Boko Haram: "This is a worrying situation that today challenges the entire international community in its fight against terrorism," affirming his country's commitment to send troops alongside neighbouring countries.

a1716.speaker: United States Agency for International Development (USAID)
a1716.name: United States Agency for International Development (USAID)
a1716.speech: Announced the suspension of the disbursement of new funds and the distribution of funds under Development Objective Agreements (DOAG) until the review of USAID-funded country assistance programmes is completed, within 90 days starting from January 24, 2025, a review process aimed at ensuring that foreign aid aligns with President Donald Trump's foreign policy agenda.

a1716.speaker: Regnant Kivenge (Kivinge), Chairman of Mafinga Town Council
a1716.name: Regnant Kivenge (Kivinge)
a1716.title: Chairman of Mafinga Town Council
a1716.speech: Said on February 8, 2025, at an ordinary session of the councillors' council reviewing second-quarter budgets for the 2024/2025 financial year, that while awaiting a government statement the council had organised itself and taken firm steps to set aside 15.6 million shillings to reassure the beneficiaries who had been served by the Benjamin William Mkapa Foundation and the USAID Afya Yangu Programme. "Our council had about 73 employees in these institutions; we asked the chief medical officer to look at the essential areas where reductions would not have an impact, thus bringing the number to 26 employees whom we will continue to use and pay with that amount of money which the council has decided to set aside." ; He said those employees were providing counselling services at the council's health facilities, including in HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis (TB), family planning, cervical cancer, and maternal and child health interventions, and that although the council's doctors are doing well, those workers were helping to provide maternal and child health services in order to reduce the burden on health workers, which is why they had been employed by those organisations. "These jobs will run for three months as the directive states, because the President of the United States, Trump, has given 90 days; he may think otherwise and then give answers within those months. While he is deciding what to do, the council saw that it could help in those areas so that citizens are not affected."

a1716.speaker: Regnant Kivenge (Kivinge), Chairman of Mafinga Town Council
a1716.name: Regnant Kivenge (Kivinge)
a1716.title: Chairman of Mafinga Town Council
a1716.speech: Said antiretroviral (ARV) drugs to suppress HIV are available in sufficient quantities according to the council's chief medical officer, so citizens will continue to be served as usual. "These drugs are available for that period, but after that there is the usual procedure for purchasing and ordering drugs as has always been the case, because they are obtained from the Medical Stores Department (MSD)."

a1716.speaker: Menja Kalinga, Councillor for Wambi ward
a1716.name: Menja Kalinga
a1716.title: Councillor for Wambi ward
a1716.speech: Contributing to the debate after the presentation of the AIDS Committee report, congratulated the council and the experts on the step they had taken of setting aside those funds. "I urge citizens, if they have heard any reports about the directive of the President of the United States, let me reassure them that the drugs will be there and those services will continue to be provided as usual because the council has planned well."

a1716.speaker: Kassim Majaliwa, Prime Minister of Tanzania
a1716.name: Kassim Majaliwa
a1716.title: Prime Minister of Tanzania
a1716.speech: Answering a spontaneous question in Parliament on February 6, 2025, said the government is strengthening itself to grow the economy by using available resources so as to be able to afford implementation in all important areas, including the health, education and water sectors. He said Tanzania respects foreign affairs policies and implements the agreements of those policies as agreed with the countries concerned in various areas. "We have begun to see that countries with great capacity, including the United States, and these changes are affecting some countries, and even ours may experience some effects, but for us it is important to observe foreign policies as we have agreed." ; "We have the capacity, we have natural resources, we have resources; the work we have is for Tanzanians to cooperate to ensure we use the natural resources and resources we have to build the domestic economy to enable plans and budgets to implement these things."

a1716.speaker: George Mwanisongole, Member of Parliament for Mbozi
a1716.name: George Mwanisongole
a1716.title: Member of Parliament for Mbozi
a1716.speech: Asked how the government is planning to deal with the changes in United States foreign policy that will affect the implementation of Tanzania's policies in several areas, including education and health.

a1716.speaker: Parliament of Tanzania (Bunge resolution)
a1716.name: Parliament of Tanzania (Bunge resolution)
a1716.speech: Resolved on February 4, 2025, that the government should implement a plan to obtain domestic resources to fight HIV infection and AIDS without depending on donor aid.

a1716.speaker: Elibariki Kingu, Chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and HIV/AIDS Affairs
a1716.name: Elibariki Kingu
a1716.title: Chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and HIV/AIDS Affairs
a1716.speech: Presented the committee's report on the implementation of its activities between February 2024 and February 2025, and said that a large proportion of the implementation of HIV and AIDS interventions in the country depends on donor funds from outside the country.

a1850.speaker: Maria de Fátima Manso, Mozambique's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and the Mozambican Community Abroad
a1850.name: Maria de Fátima Manso
a1850.title: Mozambique's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and the Mozambican Community Abroad
a1850.speech: Expressed Mozambique's position advocating greater engagement between the African Union and the European Union in conflict prevention and combating terrorism and violent extremism: "At this historic moment, in which the EU-AU partnership celebrates 25 years, we must invest in efforts to effectively approach conflict prevention and combating terrorism and violent extremism, in light of the African Union's African Peace and Security Architecture, which provides a solid basis in the process of creating foundations for ensuring sustainable peace in Africa." ; She stressed that "an in-depth approach to this phenomenon and other phenomena that pose threats to peace and security is of utmost importance, in order to create effective stability and the implementation of development programmes aimed at the prosperity of our countries and the well-being of the peoples of our continent".

a1850.speaker: Maria de Fátima Manso, Mozambique's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and the Mozambican Community Abroad
a1850.name: Maria de Fátima Manso
a1850.title: Mozambique's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and the Mozambican Community Abroad
a1850.speech: Stressed that the member countries of the two continental organisations should pay special attention to humanitarian assistance for displaced persons and refugees and for the general population, victims of the "consequences of threats to peace and security".

a1850.speaker: Maria de Fátima Manso, Mozambique's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and the Mozambican Community Abroad
a1850.name: Maria de Fátima Manso
a1850.title: Mozambique's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and the Mozambican Community Abroad
a1850.speech: Described to the African and European foreign ministers present at the meeting the harmful consequences of terrorist actions in Cabo Delgado province for the population and economic and social infrastructure, and thanked the member countries of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), Rwanda and the European Union for their support in the fight against terrorism and violent extremism.

a1850.speaker: Maria de Fátima Manso, Mozambique's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and the Mozambican Community Abroad
a1850.name: Maria de Fátima Manso
a1850.title: Mozambique's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and the Mozambican Community Abroad
a1850.speech: Highlighted the leadership of the President of the Republic, Daniel Chapo, in the "internal inclusive dialogue process, aimed at reforms and deepening peace and stability in the country", in the context of "building a solid and sustainable democracy, as well as a golden peace".

a1918.speaker: Prof. Sidikou Ramatou Djermakoye, Minister of Population, Social Action and National Solidarity of Niger
a1918.name: Prof. Sidikou Ramatou Djermakoye
a1918.title: Minister of Population, Social Action and National Solidarity of Niger
a1918.speech: Launched on Tuesday 19 August 2025 the activities for the celebration of World Humanitarian Day under the theme "Act for Humanity", paid tribute to the resilience of affected communities and sought to raise public awareness about humanitarian activities ; said this year's theme "calls on decision-makers to use their influence to put an end to atrocities and human suffering" ; "this day, instituted in 2008 by the United Nations General Assembly, commemorates the attack on the United Nations house in Baghdad on 19 August 2003", the aim of the commemoration being to recall the significant challenges facing humanitarian actors, notably the climate emergency.

a1918.speaker: Prof. Sidikou Ramatou Djermakoye, Minister of Population, Social Action and National Solidarity of Niger
a1918.name: Prof. Sidikou Ramatou Djermakoye
a1918.title: Minister of Population, Social Action and National Solidarity of Niger
a1918.speech: Addressed the security and humanitarian situation in Niger, marked by the actions of terrorist groups, and assured that "the government is committed to restoring security and peace throughout the territory".

a1918.speaker: Prof. Sidikou Ramatou Djermakoye, Minister of Population, Social Action and National Solidarity of Niger
a1918.name: Prof. Sidikou Ramatou Djermakoye
a1918.title: Minister of Population, Social Action and National Solidarity of Niger
a1918.speech: "This event that we are celebrating together is an opportunity for us to recall that humanitarian action must align with the ideals of the Refoundation" ; "communities must be at the heart of humanitarian action" ; "humanitarian aid accompanies, but it is the communities that initiate, guide and shape the responses to their challenges" ; "it is important to respect dignity, beyond relief, and every humanitarian intervention must preserve the dignity of the women, men and children who resist crises every day."

a1918.speaker: Issoufou Soumana, representative of the NGOs
a1918.name: Issoufou Soumana
a1918.title: representative of the NGOs
a1918.speech: In his address paid tribute to humanitarian actors and underlined the crucial role of national and local organisations in assisting populations affected by climate and security challenges in Niger ; "despite the decline in funding, NGOs have maintained their assistance; this collective effort has translated into daily assistance to millions of people in Niger."

a1918.speaker: Issoufou Soumana, representative of the NGOs
a1918.name: Issoufou Soumana
a1918.title: representative of the NGOs
a1918.speech: Insisted on the need to guarantee safe and regular humanitarian access to populations in need, while ensuring the protection of populations and humanitarian actors ; said coordination mechanisms between humanitarian actors and State services "must be strengthened", specifying that "continuous engagement and dialogue between these two parties is essential in order to ensure an effective humanitarian response, from planning to the monitoring of interventions" ; added that humanitarian work requires the contribution and collaboration of all actors — State, NGOs, communities — and that "it is together, respecting our respective roles, that we will continue to act for humanity."

a1918.speaker: Nena Lafuente, representative of the technical and financial partners (PTF)
a1918.name: Nena Lafuente
a1918.title: representative of the technical and financial partners (PTF)
a1918.speech: Stressed that "humanitarian work is a collective responsibility, framed by humanitarian principles and international humanitarian law", adding "that it requires collaboration between governments, communities and humanitarian organisations, respecting the fundamental role each one plays" ; noted that in 2024, 383 humanitarian workers were killed, the deadliest year ever recorded for humanitarian personnel, and that in 2025 to date 265 humanitarians have lost their lives, which "puts us on track to exceed this grim record".

a1918.speaker: Nena Lafuente, representative of the technical and financial partners (PTF)
a1918.name: Nena Lafuente
a1918.title: representative of the technical and financial partners (PTF)
a1918.speech: Insisted on the protection of civilians and humanitarian workers against dangers linked to conflicts and disasters, and called for "respect for international humanitarian law, particularly with regard to the protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel in times of armed conflict", while stressing the need to hold accountable those who violate international humanitarian law, ensuring that the perpetrators of violence and attacks are brought to justice.

a1918.speaker: Kinday Samba, acting Humanitarian Coordinator for Niger
a1918.name: Kinday Samba
a1918.title: acting Humanitarian Coordinator for Niger
a1918.speech: Saluted "the government's efforts to establish a climate of peace and security allowing our operations to continue in the field, despite certain constraints that should be noted" ; "Whether elsewhere in the world or here in Niger, significant challenges remain to be met" ; "this requires increased mobilisation and strengthened engagement from our bilateral and multilateral partners, as well as from all our traditional or emerging donors" ; "affected populations need our help right now; we will only be able to meet all humanitarian needs if the humanitarian community and international donors invest in supporting and empowering local and national humanitarian action."

a2238.speaker: SADC member States (request at the Conference of Finance Ministers in March, chaired by the Minister of Finance of Zimbabwe)
a2238.name: SADC member States (request at the Conference of Finance Ministers in March
a2238.title: chaired by the Minister of Finance of Zimbabwe)
a2238.speech: Requested that the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) develop a platform that showcases innovations across Africa, which can be accessed by all countries.

a2300.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF) statement
a2300.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF) statement
a2300.speech: has announced a staff-level agreement with Tanzanian authorities that would grant the country access to approximately 441 million US dollars, equivalent to 1.2tril/- in financing. IMF said in a statement on Thursday that the agreement marks the successful completion of the fifth review under the IMF's Extended Credit Facility (ECF) and the second review under the Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF).

a2300.speaker: Nicolas Blancher, IMF staff team mission chief
a2300.name: Nicolas Blancher
a2300.title: IMF staff team mission chief
a2300.speech: "I am pleased to announce that the IMF team and the Tanzanian authorities have reached a staff-level agreement on the policies needed to complete the fifth review under Tanzania's ECF-supported programme and the second review of the RSF arrangement. The IMF's Executive Board will discuss these reviews in the coming weeks."

a2300.speaker: Nicolas Blancher, IMF staff team mission chief
a2300.name: Nicolas Blancher
a2300.title: IMF staff team mission chief
a2300.speech: highlighted Tanzania's strong economic performance, noting that real GDP growth reached 5.5 per cent in 2024 and is projected to increase to 6 per cent in 2025. ; While acknowledging a favourable economic outlook, Mr Blancher cautioned that risks are tilted to the downside due to an uncertain external environment, including potential slowdowns in the global economy and trade, geoeconomics fragmentation, further conflict intensification in the Democratic Republic of Congo and reduced foreign development assistance.

a2300.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2300.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2300.speech: noted that fiscal consolidation is expected to pause in the current fiscal year 2024/2025 following the adoption of a supplementary budget in February 2025, which aims to increase public spending by about 0.4 per cent of GDP on education, health, clearance of domestic arrears and other priority areas. The Fund stressed the importance of resuming growth-friendly fiscal consolidation in 2025/2026 fiscal year to preserve debt sustainability and rebuild fiscal space, particularly given pressing social spending needs.

a2300.speaker: Tanzanian authorities
a2300.name: Tanzanian authorities
a2300.speech: have committed to reducing the domestic primary deficit by 0.4 percentage points of GDP to 0.8 per cent in 2025/2026 through revenue measures yielding 0.9 per cent of GDP, while safeguarding priority social spending at 7.1 per cent of GDP.

a2300.speaker: IMF mission
a2300.name: IMF mission
a2300.speech: concurred with BOT's decision to maintain the Central Bank Rate (CBR) at 6 per cent, considering inflation remains below the 5 per cent target. They believe this stance will help preserve price stability. The mission also underscored the importance of continuing to allow exchange rate flexibility and conducting foreign exchange interventions in line with the BOT's policy.

a2300.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2300.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2300.speech: stressed the critical need to dedicate sufficient resources to education and health for a young and rapidly growing population and to foster an enabling environment for private sector-led growth and job creation, to achieve the ambitious goals outlined in the Tanzania Vision 2050. Key structural reform priorities identified include further efforts to improve access to finance, streamline business regulations and strengthen judicial and anticorruption institutions. The IMF also highlighted the importance of continuing the implementation of climate reforms, supported by the RSF, to enhance climate resilience and sustainability.

a2484.speaker: Ben Nangombe, Executive Director, Ministry of Health and Social Services (MoHSS)
a2484.name: Ben Nangombe
a2484.title: Executive Director, Ministry of Health and Social Services (MoHSS)
a2484.speech: Said HIV prevalence among pregnant women has declined from 22% in 2002 to 14% last year; revealed that 98% of all pregnant women in Namibia attend antenatal care, and more than 90% of them deliver at hospitals, that antiretroviral therapy coverage among HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding mothers stands at 98%, and viral load suppression is around 97% ; "As a result, the rate of mother-to-child transmission has reduced from 13.7% in 2010. The identification of HIV and provisional lifelong ARV among pregnant and breastfeeding women on ARV porfilaxis for their exposed infants has been the backbone of the TCE programme. HIV testing services are offered to all pregnant women who attend ANC, and in recent years, HIV testing among pregnant women has remained as high as 98%."

a2484.speaker: Kirsten Moeller Jensen, Managing Director of Development Aid from People to People
a2484.name: Kirsten Moeller Jensen
a2484.title: Managing Director of Development Aid from People to People
a2484.speech: "When you see the babies with their mothers here, our mission is to support the mothers both to link them to ANC services before birth and after birth, following them for 18 months to make sure they do the right thing so that their babies stay negative, and in 2022, we had a 100% success rate doing that with more than 3000 mothers."

a2484.speaker: Dr John Nkengasong, U.S. Global AIDS Coordinator
a2484.name: Dr John Nkengasong
a2484.title: U.S. Global AIDS Coordinator
a2484.speech: Commended Namibia for its achievements in the fight against HIV among pregnant and breastfeeding women: "There is absolutely no amount of data you put out in public that will drive home what we are seeing here; this is so personal. Remember where we were 20 years ago? They will probably be sitting here with no child or mother because they were born to HIV-infected mothers. This is what it means to offer hope to the people, the community, and the nation; this is nation-building. We are all here to recognise that in as much as one of our priorities for Pepfar is recognising the inequity gaps that exist in the children's population, the adolescent girls and young women, and key populations, this is a clear demonstration of how you are filling that gap."

a2529.speaker: Janvier Yahouédéhou, member of the Beninese National Assembly
a2529.name: Janvier Yahouédéhou
a2529.title: member of the Beninese National Assembly
a2529.speech: On the procurement procedures, said the government's single-source (gré à gré) contracts amounted to insider dealing: “it was after the Coordinator of the PPMA project was appointed on 23 April 2008 that several companies benefiting from these single-source contracts were created”, citing LASAVANE (created 22 January 2009, awarded 1.45 billion CFA francs), ADJITI Sarl (created 05-11-2008, awarded 874,000,000 CFA francs) and SPL Sarl (created 25 August 2008, awarded 1,090,010,000 CFA francs four months later); “That is what I call insider dealing” ; He said the companies belong to the same individuals, that Mr Ange Olivier Boko passed himself off to the Canadians as Managing Director of SPL Sarl while in reality being the owner of CDGA, which obtained a 3.3 billion CFA franc contract, and that Boko is the husband of the younger sister of Nieri Bio Romain Stéphane, manager of SPL Sarl: “these companies were created for the purposes of the cause” ; He recalled that article 46 of law 2004-18 on public procurement requires that authorised single-source contracts not exceed 10 per cent of the entity's total procurement, whereas “the totality of the acquisitions by the government was made by single-source procurement.”

a2529.speaker: Janvier Yahouédéhou, member of the Beninese National Assembly
a2529.name: Janvier Yahouédéhou
a2529.title: member of the Beninese National Assembly
a2529.speech: On the quality of the machines, said that of 18 sixty-horsepower tractors delivered in Atacora/Donga, 5 were already immobilised by oil leaks, 2 parked with broken crankshafts and damaged connecting rods, and another with diesel leaks only three months after delivery, and that machines inspected at Ouinhi, Zagnanado, Cové, Zogbodomey and Djidja were all parked and in places rusted; he asked where the pre-shipment inspection documents attesting that the technical characteristics were respected are, and said: “If I am told that these are new machines, that means that in reality the quality of these new machines is inferior to the quality of the used machine that I had bought” ; On the stump cutters (gyro-shredders), he said the GYROTRAC branch producing them no longer exists, showing the bankruptcy notice from the Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy of Canada dated 25 May 2010 and documents from the US Bankruptcy Court in South Carolina, and noted that GYROTRAC was declared bankrupt on 23 December 2009, the very day its CEO was in Benin.

a2529.speaker: Janvier Yahouédéhou, member of the Beninese National Assembly
a2529.name: Janvier Yahouédéhou
a2529.title: member of the Beninese National Assembly
a2529.speech: On the truthfulness of the prices, said a 30-horsepower tractor costs 3,723 US dollars (1,897,204 CFA francs) in China while the PPMA declared 9,000,000 CFA francs per unit for 250 units, and a 60-horsepower tractor costs 7,763 US dollars (2,936,000 CFA francs) while the PPMA declared 12 million per unit for 200 units; he said the four stump cutters were invoiced by GYROTRAC at 742,523 US dollars, some 384 million CFA francs with freight, but that the Beninese State disbursed 1,090,000,000 CFA francs, and that the invoice was re-issued to a screen company, HIGH TECH DETECTION SYSTEM in Massy, France, “in order to increase the amount to be invoiced to Benin so as to be able to deceive the Beninese tax authorities and play on the margin” ; He rejected claims that he was being manipulated and misinformed: “I am in direct contact with the United States and Canada on this file. I have all the information and all the documents.”

a2529.speaker: Janvier Yahouédéhou, member of the Beninese National Assembly
a2529.name: Janvier Yahouédéhou
a2529.title: member of the Beninese National Assembly
a2529.speech: Addressing the Head of State, said: “I would respectfully ask the Head of State to launch an international commission of inquiry at his level, which will also give you more details than this”, and reassured everyone that “contrary to all that is being said, Yahouédéou Janvier has no problem with anyone whatsoever”, recalling that he had said on 19 February 2009 at Bohicon during the UNDP congress that what binds him to Yayi Boni is good governance, and that normally the Head of State should have anticipated and set up a commission of inquiry seven months ago.

a2529.speaker: The Minister, speaking on behalf of the Head of State of Benin
a2529.name: The Minister
a2529.title: speaking on behalf of the Head of State of Benin
a2529.speech: justified the choice of single-source (gré à gré) contracts by the fact that the provisions of Law No. 2004-18 of 27 August 2004 on the public procurement code allow, among other things, that when the execution of works, the delivery of supplies or the provision of services is the object of a monopoly, one is obliged to turn to those companies; it was also said that because there was urgency, the strategic choice was made to place orders by mutual agreement.

a2529.speaker: A parliamentary colleague (anonymous deputy)
a2529.name: A parliamentary colleague (anonymous deputy)
a2529.speech: already said that since 1 December 2009, when documents that would allow deputies to understand this file were requested, nothing has been sent.

a2529.speaker: Director General of CeRPA Atacora/Donga (letter No. 608 of 8 September 2009 to the PPMA Coordinator)
a2529.name: Director General of CeRPA Atacora/Donga (letter No. 608 of 8 September 2009 to the PPMA Coordinator)
a2529.speech: takes stock of the breakdowns on the machines delivered in June 2009, three months after delivery: of 18 tractors of 60 horsepower delivered, 5 were already immobilised because of oil leaks, 2 parked because of broken crankshafts and damaged connecting rods, and another because of diesel leaks; among the 30-horsepower machines, damaged connecting rod bearings, broken exhausts and jamming of the hydraulic lift lever.

a2529.speaker: Steve Quirion, third shareholder (5%) of GYROTRAC (sworn statement in the minutes of the US Bankruptcy Court of South Carolina)
a2529.name: Steve Quirion
a2529.title: third shareholder (5%) of GYROTRAC (sworn statement in the minutes of the US Bankruptcy Court of South Carolina)
a2529.speech: “GYROTRAC is a group of three companies. The companies also assisted each other in their routine activities according to their needs. For example, during the year preceding the bankruptcy, GYROTRAC USA had arranged a sale to a client in Benin in Africa. GYROTRAC USA had equipment in its inventory whereas GYROTRAC WEST COAST had none. In order to facilitate the international transaction, GYROTRAC settled the inventory financing credit with BB&T and transferred the equipment to GYROTRAC WEST COAST without first having received payment. GYROTRAC then secured the sale of the equipment to the client in Africa. The machines were sold under the name of GYROTRAC WEST COAST, which received the funds, although the labour and most of the details concerning the sale and handling of the equipment were provided by GYROTRAC USA. In accordance with its loan and guarantee agreement with GYROTRAC WEST COAST, the Bank of Montreal seized the net proceeds of these transactions.”

a2627.speaker: NGOs Save the Children, Plan International, Oxfam and Action Against Hunger
a2627.name: NGOs Save the Children
a2627.title: Plan International, Oxfam and Action Against Hunger
a2627.speech: Say the catastrophe is “final and inevitable,” manufactured by Israel and with effects that will be irreversible for many children of the Palestinian enclave.

a2627.speaker: Inger Ashing, Executive Director of Save the Children International
a2627.name: Inger Ashing
a2627.title: Executive Director of Save the Children International
a2627.speech: “The world has been watching while children have suffered the unthinkable for almost two years in Gaza, and now we have confirmation that hundreds of thousands are being slowly condemned to starvation” ; “All of Gaza is being systematically and deliberately starved, and children are paying the highest price. The world has failed to act. This man-made famine is the final and inevitable result of the use of starvation as a weapon of war by the Government of Israel” ; “There is no world leader who did not know that this was going to happen.”

a2627.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), Rome-based UN body
a2627.name: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC)
a2627.title: Rome-based UN body
a2627.speech: Confirmed that a famine is under way in Gaza and placed it at phase 5, which implies extreme lack of access to food and drinking water, large-scale forced displacement and a high mortality rate; according to the declaration, the situation will extend by the end of September to the provinces of Deir el-Balah (centre) and Khan Yunis (south).

a2627.speaker: Experts (food security specialists)
a2627.name: Experts (food security specialists)
a2627.speech: Warned that 500,000 people were in a catastrophic situation.

a2627.speaker: Humanitarian groups
a2627.name: Humanitarian groups
a2627.speech: Denounced that the restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of food and other kinds of aid into the Gaza Strip, together with the military offensive, were causing high levels of hunger among Palestinian civilians, especially children.

a2627.speaker: Tom Fletcher, United Nations humanitarian affairs coordination chief
a2627.name: Tom Fletcher
a2627.title: United Nations humanitarian affairs coordination chief
a2627.speech: Charged in Geneva that the famine in Gaza “could have been avoided” without “Israel’s systematic obstruction” ; “This famine will and must haunt us all.”

a2627.speaker: Action Against Hunger (NGO)
a2627.name: Action Against Hunger (NGO)
a2627.speech: Warned of a rapid deterioration of the situation; its teams in Deir el-Balah warned that they are currently recording the highest number of cases of severe acute malnutrition since the start of their nutritional operations in Gaza in 2024; warned that local food production is almost impossible since “only 1.5% of Gaza’s arable land is accessible to the population and undamaged,” and added that “inflation has triggered a 4,000% increase in the prices of essential foods compared with pre-war prices, which makes basic necessities unaffordable.”

a2627.speaker: Mahmud Alsaqqa, Oxfam Food Security and Livelihoods Coordinator
a2627.name: Mahmud Alsaqqa
a2627.title: Oxfam Food Security and Livelihoods Coordinator
a2627.speech: Attributed the crisis “in its entirety” to Israel’s blockade of the entry of food and vital aid into the territory, “a terrible consequence of Israeli violence and its use of starvation as a weapon of war” ; “The people of the Gaza Strip are suffering deliberate starvation, relentless bombardment and forced displacement. All of this is part of the Israeli genocide.”

a2627.speaker: Plan International (NGO)
a2627.name: Plan International (NGO)
a2627.speech: Said it managed to bring 10 trucks of food into Gaza since 6 August, enough to feed 45,000 people for three days, but warned that much more is needed to meet the needs of a starving population.

a2627.speaker: Unni Krishnan, Global Humanitarian Director of Plan International
a2627.name: Unni Krishnan
a2627.title: Global Humanitarian Director of Plan International
a2627.speech: Stressed that “the dire consequences of Israel’s use of starvation as a weapon of war and of the blockade of humanitarian aid are devastatingly evident to all” ; “No conflict should reach this point. What we are seeing today in Gaza is a wholly manufactured and avoidable catastrophe that is leaving more than a million Palestinian children, and 2.2 million people in total, struggling to survive” ; “The famine in Gaza is not a logistical or aid failure, it is the result of a brutal war and deliberate starvation” ; “We demand, without delay, an immediate and sustained ceasefire, a total end to the supply of weapons to Israel and the complete lifting of Israel’s illegal blockade on humanitarian aid.”

a2627.speaker: Gaza local authorities (casualty figures)
a2627.name: Gaza local authorities (casualty figures)
a2627.speech: Updated figures, which the UN considers reliable, state that the war has so far caused 62,263 deaths, mostly civilians, and at least 157,114 injured, in addition to thousands missing and several thousand more who died of disease, infection and hunger; and that the Army has so far killed 2,060 and injured at least 15,448 Palestinian civilians at aid distribution points.

a2627.speaker: Special UN commission (end of 2024)
a2627.name: Special UN commission (end of 2024)
a2627.speech: Had accused Israel of genocide in Gaza and of using starvation as a weapon of war.

a2627.speaker: South Africa (before the International Court of Justice)
a2627.name: South Africa (before the International Court of Justice)
a2627.speech: Denounced the same situation before the International Court of Justice, a classification likewise used by international and Israeli human rights organisations.

a2789.speaker: Fiona Ritchie, UK High Commissioner to Malawi
a2789.name: Fiona Ritchie
a2789.title: UK High Commissioner to Malawi
a2789.speech: Says the UK government will continue providing different support to Malawi. Ritchie said they have heard loud and clear that what people want from the UK is support for modern solutions to intractable problems, and they will continue to do that. “We will continue supporting new technologies, be that in solar power for health centres or looking at how social protection support reaches individuals through mobile money transfer through world-class research that tackles the global challenges we face like Covid, or through the collaboration of our academics and thought leaders,” she explained.

a2789.speaker: Fiona Ritchie, UK High Commissioner to Malawi
a2789.name: Fiona Ritchie
a2789.title: UK High Commissioner to Malawi
a2789.speech: Said the partnership with Malawi is not about charity or dependence. “A modem partnership goes beyond aid. In the future, I hope to see more collaboration in areas such as technology and trade to deliver our shared objectives,” she explained. Ritchie also commended the good relationship that Malawi has with the UK.

a2789.speaker: Nancy Tembo, Malawi Minister of Foreign Affairs
a2789.name: Nancy Tembo
a2789.title: Malawi Minister of Foreign Affairs
a2789.speech: Said over the years, Britain has remained one of Malawi's major development partners, complementing government efforts in providing social services and addressing bottlenecks along the country's development trajectory. “British support covers all critical sectors of our society including health, education, macro-economic stability, climate change, governance, and public financial management, among others. In public financial management, the UK is supporting us in delivering inclusive economic growth, as well as leveraging expertise in tackling unsustainable debt, which helped us to qualify for the International Monetary Fund's Extended Credit Facility,” she explained.

a2789.speaker: Nancy Tembo, Malawi Minister of Foreign Affairs
a2789.name: Nancy Tembo
a2789.title: Malawi Minister of Foreign Affairs
a2789.speech: Noted that Malawi is very grateful to His Majesty's government for tripling its Official Development Assistance (ODA) to Malawi from £16,340,000 in the 2023/2024 financial year to £51,000,000 for the 2024/2025 financial year. “This significant increase reflects the importance of the UK's partnership with Malawi and the UK's commitment to supporting Malawi's Vision 2063. Therefore, I wish to express our sincere gratitude to His Majesty's Government for the tremendous support the UK continues to relentlessly provide to Malawi,” said Tembo.

a2966.speaker: International Rescue Committee (IRC) (statement)
a2966.name: International Rescue Committee (IRC) (statement)
a2966.speech: “Recent heavy rainfall has led to flooding, resulting in destruction of crops, loss of livestock and displacement. Swarms of multiplying desert locusts have also been destroying pastures and crops, leading to further food insecurity. Some areas are recording admissions for severe acute malnutrition at 50% higher than for the same period last year. A massive twelve fold increase in Covid-19 cases between June and September is further compounding needs as families have been unable to obtain income or access food due to movement restrictions.”

a2966.speaker: International Rescue Committee (IRC) (statement)
a2966.name: International Rescue Committee (IRC) (statement)
a2966.speech: Said that IRC is working to safeguard the lives of affected and at-risk communities from the COVID-19 pandemic by raising community awareness on COVID-19 risk factors, providing personal protective equipment, and building and installing water points to help people practice preventative methods ; “The IRC is assisting desert locust and flood-affected households with multi-purpose cash transfer and non-food items to fill food security gaps and provide relief.”

a2966.speaker: Frank McManus, IRC Ethiopia Country Director
a2966.name: Frank McManus
a2966.title: IRC Ethiopia Country Director
a2966.speech: “The multiple issues of flooding, locusts, intercommunal violence and COVID-19 are highly concerning given the already massive humanitarian needs in the country. The slowdown of the economy and lockdown restrictions mean that people have not been able to access income and there is an upward pressure on food prices.” ; “Over 19 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance in Ethiopia. At four times the number of people displaced in 2019, as a result of the flooding, more than 300,000 people have been displaced in 2020 and have had their homes and livelihoods lost or damaged. A total of over 1 million people have been adversely affected by the floods overall... The IRC is providing essential support through distributions of non-food items, including emergency shelter, household goods, hygiene kits, and cash assistance to over 36,500 affected people.” ; “Despite the IRC’s work, the unmet humanitarian needs are still great. With more funding for our work, we will be able to reach even more people with the critical support they so desperately need after losing their homes and livelihoods.”

a2972.speaker: Samia Mahgoub, Country Director of FSVC-SHIGA
a2972.name: Samia Mahgoub
a2972.title: Country Director of FSVC-SHIGA
a2972.speech: Said this incubation cycle brings together 14 CSOs working on various health themes, particularly primary health care, the fight against cancer, and the inclusion of people with disabilities in the health system ; “These CSOs, which operate in the regions of Dosso, Maradi, Niamey, Tahoua, Tillabéri and Zinder, were selected at the end of a transparent and rigorous process. The criteria of gender, inclusion and regional balance were carefully taken into account in the final selection of these organisations. This is an opportunity for me to congratulate them on this selection and to salute their commitment throughout the assessment of their capacities and their training needs.”

a2972.speaker: Samia Mahgoub, Country Director of FSVC-SHIGA
a2972.name: Samia Mahgoub
a2972.title: Country Director of FSVC-SHIGA
a2972.speech: Stressed that over the 12 months of incubation, these CSOs will benefit from numerous training sessions on health themes as well as in advocacy techniques, digital communication, project design and resource mobilisation, and monitoring and evaluation ; “This capacity building will begin as early as tomorrow with the holding of a three-day training workshop on public health policies and Social and Behaviour Change Communication (SBCC).”

a2972.speaker: Samia Mahgoub, Country Director of FSVC-SHIGA
a2972.name: Samia Mahgoub
a2972.title: Country Director of FSVC-SHIGA
a2972.speech: Reiterated the thanks of Financial Services Volunteers Corps (FSVC) to the American Government and to USAID for their ever-renewed support to their organisation in implementing the incubation process in Niger from July 2019 to today.
